title: Sliding Expiration
description: Implement sliding expiration to keep active users logged in while still expiring inactive sessions.

data.text: Welcome to this comprehensive guide on **Sliding Expiration**. Implement sliding expiration to keep active users logged in while still expiring inactive sessions. In today's rapidly evolving technology landscape, understanding this topic is crucial for any developer looking to build robust, scalable, and maintainable applications. This lesson will take you from fundamental concepts to advanced implementations, providing you with practical knowledge you can apply immediately. Whether you are a beginner taking your first steps or an experienced developer looking to deepen your expertise, this guide has something valuable for you. We will explore theoretical foundations, practical implementations, real-world scenarios, and common pitfalls to avoid. By the end of this lesson, you will have a thorough understanding of Sliding Expiration and be confident in applying it to your projects.

blocks.text: Sliding expiration is a session management strategy where the expiration time of a token is extended each time the user is actively using the application. Instead of a fixed expiration date, each refresh or activity event pushes the expiration forward by a configured window. Inactive users are eventually logged out, while active users remain authenticated seamlessly.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of sliding expiration like a library book renewal. As long as you keep renewing the book, you can keep it. If you stop renewing, the book eventually expires and must be returned.

cards.title: Absolute Expiration
cards.description: The token expires at a fixed time regardless of activity.
cons: Active users get logged out unexpectedly
Poor user experience for long tasks

cards.title: Sliding Expiration
cards.description: The token expiration moves forward with each use, keeping active sessions alive.
cons: Inactive sessions can live indefinitely without limits

blocks.text: With sliding expiration, each time the client refreshes its access token using a refresh token, the refresh token expiration is pushed forward. For example, if the sliding window is 30 minutes and the refresh token is used at minute 25 of its life, it now expires at minute 55. If the refresh token is never used again, it expires at its original time.

  New Expiration          :a2, after m1, 30m
  section Without Refresh
  User inactive           :a3, 00:00, 30m
  Token expires at 30m    :milestone, m2, 30m, 0m

blocks.text: Sliding expiration is implemented in the refresh token endpoint. When a refresh request is received, check the current refresh token expiration. If it is within a certain threshold of expiring, issue a new refresh token with a fresh expiration. Otherwise, return a new access token but keep the same refresh token. Always enforce a maximum absolute lifetime to prevent tokens from sliding forever.

blocks.title: Sliding expiration refresh endpoint
blocks.content: Express implementation that extends refresh token expiration on each use.

blocks.title: Guidelines for Window Size
items: Match the window to your access token lifetime plus a small buffer (e.g., access token = 15 min, window = 30 min)
Shorter windows force more frequent refreshes, improving security but reducing convenience
Longer windows keep users logged in longer but increase the window for token theft
Consider user expectations: if users expect to work for hours, use a longer window

blocks.title: Maximum Absolute Lifetime
blocks.text: Always enforce a maximum absolute lifetime on refresh tokens, even with sliding expiration. Without this limit, an active user could stay logged in indefinitely, which violates most security policies.

Clients should proactively refresh access tokens before they expire. A common pattern is to refresh when the access token has less than 5 minutes remaining. When the server returns a new refresh token, the client must update its stored token. If the refresh fails, the client should redirect the user to the login page.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
points: Sliding expiration extends the refresh token lifetime with each use
Combine sliding expiration with a maximum absolute lifetime
Implement sliding logic on the server during token refresh
Proactively refresh access tokens on the client before they expire
Set the sliding window to match access token lifetime plus a buffer
blocks.takeaway: Sliding expiration keeps active users authenticated while still ensuring inactive sessions eventually expire, striking the right balance between security and user experience.

data.text: Common Mistakes to Avoid

Even experienced developers can fall into these traps when working with **Sliding Expiration**. Being aware of these common mistakes will help you write better code and avoid costly debugging sessions:

items: **Over-Engineering**: Using advanced features of Sliding Expiration when a simple solution suffices. Always start with the simplest approach that meets your requirements and add complexity only when justified.
**Ignoring Edge Cases**: Failing to handle null values, empty states, and boundary conditions leads to runtime errors and poor user experience.
**Copy-Paste Without Understanding**: Using code snippets without fully understanding their implications creates hidden bugs and security vulnerabilities.
**Neglecting Testing**: Assuming code works without tests is a recipe for production incidents. Write tests that verify behavior and prevent regressions.
**Performance Blindness**: Ignoring performance implications until they become critical issues. Profile early and optimize based on data, not assumptions.
**Hardcoding Configuration**: Embedding values directly in code instead of using environment variables and configuration files.
**Tight Coupling**: Creating dependencies that make code difficult to test, modify, or reuse. Favor composition over inheritance.
**Inconsistent Error Handling**: Mixing different error handling patterns makes code unpredictable and hard to debug.

data.text: Performance Considerations

Performance is a critical aspect of any production application. When implementing **Sliding Expiration**, consider these optimization strategies to ensure your application remains fast and responsive:

items: **Lazy Loading**: Defer non-critical operations until they are actually needed to reduce initial load time.
**Caching**: Implement intelligent caching strategies to avoid redundant computations and network requests.
**Memoization**: Cache results of expensive function calls to improve performance for repeated operations.
**Batch Processing**: Group multiple operations together to reduce overhead and improve throughput.
**Resource Management**: Properly clean up resources, event listeners, and subscriptions to prevent memory leaks.
**Profiling**: Use performance profiling tools to identify bottlenecks before optimizing.
**Bundle Size**: Minimize dependencies and use tree-shaking to reduce application bundle size.
**Network Optimization**: Reduce payload sizes, use compression, and implement efficient data fetching strategies.

data.text: Security Considerations
Security should never be an afterthought. When implementing **Sliding Expiration**, keep these security best practices in mind to protect your application and users:

items: **Input Validation**: Always validate and sanitize user input to prevent injection attacks.
**Authentication and Authorization**: Implement proper access controls and verify user permissions.
**Secrets Management**: Never hardcode API keys, passwords, or tokens. Use environment variables and secret management services.
**HTTPS**: Always use HTTPS in production to encrypt data in transit.
**Content Security Policy**: Implement CSP headers to mitigate XSS attacks.
**Dependency Scanning**: Regularly scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities.
**Rate Limiting**: Protect APIs from abuse with appropriate rate limiting.
**Audit Logging**: Log security-relevant events for monitoring and incident response.
